questions.title: Original pair orientation
questions.prompt: A log keeps only `chosen/rejected`; the original A/B order is lost. Which checks become impossible?
questions.explanation: You can no longer measure positional bias honestly, reconstruct the observed 0/1 label in the original orientation, or build a sound calibration set. Store the original order, candidate identifiers, and the annotator decision.

questions.title: Comparison-graph connectivity
questions.prompt: Two sets of responses were never compared across sets. Can their absolute BT scores be compared?
questions.explanation: No. Each connected component admits an independent additive score shift. Bridging comparisons or an external anchor are required; centering within components does not create cross-component information.

questions.title: Row split without prompt isolation
questions.prompt: Why can a random row split overstate reward-model quality?
questions.explanation: Pairs from the same prompt may appear in both train and test. The model can exploit prompt, generator, or template identity instead of transferring the criterion. Use a prompt-disjoint split and add temporal/domain slices.

questions.title: Calibration on the test set
questions.prompt: Temperature scaling is fitted on the same set used to report ECE. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: The estimate is optimistic because the test set tuned the calibrator. Use train, calibration, and evaluation splits; fit temperature on calibration and report metrics on untouched evaluation data.

questions.title: Accuracy without calibration
questions.prompt: Two RMs have the same pair accuracy but different log loss. What does that show?
questions.explanation: They get the sign right equally often but differ in probability quality and confidence. Lower log loss usually indicates better probabilistic predictions; accuracy cannot reveal that.

questions.title: Averaging raw ensemble scores
questions.prompt: Why is raw-score averaging across independently trained RMs unsafe?
questions.explanation: Each score has an arbitrary origin and scale. Calibrate each model on a common calibration set, convert margins to probabilities, and aggregate probabilities. Ensemble spread is a diagnostic, not automatically a confidence interval.

questions.title: Proxy overoptimization
questions.prompt: Proxy score rises with Best-of-N while independent utility falls after N=32. What follows?
questions.explanation: Selection pressure is exploiting a proxy direction. Cap the search pressure, add independent metrics and fresh labels, test distribution shift, and never select N using the proxy alone.

questions.title: Judge swap test
questions.prompt: An LLM judge chooses position A 70% of the time and preserves the same textual winner after swapping only 55% of the time. What is diagnosed?
questions.explanation: Strong position sensitivity. Evaluate both orientations, aggregate explicitly, inspect ties, and include independent human audit.

questions.title: Soft tie
questions.prompt: Annotators split 6:4. Why does a hard label of 1 discard information?
questions.explanation: It makes a weak majority indistinguishable from unanimity. A soft target of 0.6 or an annotator model preserves uncertainty and supports calibration analysis.

questions.title: Reward model versus cost model
questions.prompt: Can a separate cost model always be replaced by negative reward?
questions.explanation: No. Utility and risk may depend on different features, thresholds, and error costs. Log and validate them separately; critical constraints should not be compensated by high utility.

questions.title: Fresh policy responses
questions.prompt: Why is RM evaluation only on old candidates insufficient before RL?
questions.explanation: Optimization shifts the response distribution into regions not covered by the old set. Evaluate fresh current-policy generations, generator/domain slices, and independent labels.

questions.title: Outcome and process reward
questions.prompt: When are whole-answer and step-level scores not interchangeable?
questions.explanation: An outcome score does not locate the faulty step, while local scores need not compose into a correct whole-answer value. A PRM needs its own annotation semantics and validation.
